articles.title: Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov is launching a defense technology company backed by Palantir
articles.summary: Tech News News: Palantir CEO Alex Karp stepping in as the first lead investor in a new defense technology company founded by former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhail.
articles.body: Palantir CEO Alex Karp stepping in as the first lead investor in a new defense technology company founded by former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedoro. According to a report by CNBC, the size of Karp’s investment has not been disclosed, but Fedorov’s press office confirmed the partnership, saying details of cooperation with Palantir will be announced gradually. In a video posted by Fedorov on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter), Karp praised the venture, saying it could bring Ukraine’s wartime knowledge and experience “as a product to allied countries.” He added: “You and your colleagues are launching a company that I think will be defining for the world.”Alex Karp backed defense company turning wartime experience into a productThe company’s name, specific technologies, and the extent of Karp’s involvement have not yet been disclosed. Palantir did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Fedorov’s office said the venture will build on lessons learned during Ukraine’s war with Russia, where drones, artificial intelligence, and battlefield software have played a critical role.A war reshaping military technologyThe launch comes as Ukraine's ongoing war with Russia continues to accelerate the development and battlefield deployment of technologies including drones, artificial intelligence, and military software. Fedorov, long known as a vocal advocate for using technology to modernize Ukraine's military, said the new company would apply lessons learned during the war to build technology usable by both Ukraine and its allied partners.Fedorov, 35, said in a statement: “During the full-scale war, our team gained unique experience working with defense technologies in Ukraine and seeing firsthand how technology is transforming modern warfare.” He added that the company will aim to apply those lessons to products usable by both Ukraine and its allies.Fedorov's abrupt exit from governmentFedorov, 35, was removed from his role as defense minister by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in July as part of a broader government reshuffle, after serving in the position for just six months. His removal sparked public protests in Ukraine at the time.What Fedorov has been doing since leaving governmentSince exiting government, Fedorov has been actively courting US investors and technology executives as he pursues a series of defense-focused ventures. He is separately seeking U.S. backing for a defense technology investment fund targeting areas including battlefield robotics, interceptor drones, and AI-enabled missile systems, according to a Financial Times report published last week.Fedorov built relationships with several prominent U.S. tech executives during the war. articles.title: After Google, Apple Maps changes 'Lake Ontario' name to 'Lake America' for US users; Trump calls move 'ratified, binding'
articles.summary: US News: US President Donald Trump on Wednesday (local time) said his renaming of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” was “ratified and binding” after Apple updated.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump on Wednesday (local time) said his renaming of Lake Ontario to “Lake America” was “ratified and binding” after Apple updated the water body’s name for users in the US, making it the second major US tech company to adopt the new name.“Apple Maps has just announced that it has changed the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America,” Trump posted on his Truth Social platform, adding that the "very important" change was now “complete, ratified, and binding.”Google had updated the name on Google Maps on August 29, following the US Geographic Names Information System (GNIS) formally changing the lake’s name in America.According to Google, “Lake America” will appear for users in the United States, while users in Canada will continue to see “Lake Ontario.” Users elsewhere will see both names, with “Lake America” in parentheses after “Lake Ontario”, following Google’s policy for water bodies with different names in different countries.Also Read | Google renames 'Lake Ontario' to 'Lake America' in US; company's 'update' on what users in America, Canada and 'rest of the world' will seeThe move follows an executive order signed by Trump directing the US Department of the Interior to update federal maps and databases to refer to Lake Ontario as “Lake America” within the US, amid a major trade dispute with Canada.However, the order applies only to US federal agencies and has no authority over Canadian territory or international hydrographic standards.Lake Ontario is shared by the United States and Canada and is governed by the Boundary Waters Treaty. It is one of the five "Great Lakes" along the US-Canada border.The renaming has drawn strong opposition in Canada. After Prime Minister Mark Carney rejected the move, Ontario Premier Doug Ford unveiled a large sign along the Canadian shore reading “Lake Ontario. Now and Always” in English and French.The dispute comes amid broader economic and political tensions between the two countries. The Trump administration imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods, prompting Ottawa to announce retaliatory tariffs on US exports. Following the breakdown of trade talks, Trump cited “trade frustrations” in connection with the name change.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Quote of the day by Chuck Feeney: "I don't dislike money, but there's only so much money you can use" - a timeless lesson in knowing when you have enough
articles.summary: US News: Money is often treated as the clearest possible measure of success. People work toward higher salaries, bigger homes and greater financial security, a.
articles.body: Money is often treated as the clearest possible measure of success. People work toward higher salaries, bigger homes and greater financial security, and rarely stop to question the assumption underneath all of it. Chuck Feeney, the Irish-American businessman who made billions through the Duty Free Shoppers business, took a genuinely different approach to wealth. "I don't dislike money," he said, "but there's only so much money you can use." Feeney never rejected wealth outright, and he never pretended money was unimportant. What he genuinely questioned was how much a single person actually needs for themselves, and what can honestly be done with the rest of it. That question became particularly striking because Feeney went on to give away almost his entire fortune while he was still alive, rather than waiting until after his death, directing billions of dollars toward causes he genuinely cared about through his own foundation over several decades.Quote of the day by Chuck Feeney"I don't dislike money, but there's only so much money you can use"The real anecdote that captures why Chuck Feeney did thisFeeney once described a specific moment that stayed with him for the rest of his life. "I watched a little girl cover her face up and leave her hands in front of her mouth," he said. "I saw that girl after surgery, and she was smiling... that's a great source of satisfaction." The moment reportedly came through his support for reconstructive surgery for children born with cleft palates, funded through his philanthropic foundation, Atlantic Philanthropies. That single image, a child finally comfortable enough to smile without hiding her own face, genuinely explains far more about his real motivation than any abstract statement about wealth ever could.What did Chuck Feeney actually mean by this quoteFeeney's statement is genuinely straightforward. He acknowledged that money has real value, while arguing there is a practical limit to how much any one person can actually use for themselves. A person can buy a bigger house or a more expensive car, but there is a genuine point where additional wealth stops actually changing everyday life in any meaningful way. For Feeney, that raised a bigger real question. If a person genuinely has more money than they realistically need, what should actually happen to the rest of it? His own answer was philanthropy, and rather than waiting until the end of his life to distribute his wealth, he chose to give it away while he was still alive to see the actual results. "I believe strongly in 'giving while living,'" he said. "I see little reason to delay giving when so much good can be achieved through supporting worthwhile causes today. Besides, it's a lot more fun to give while you live than to give while you are dead." He put the same idea even more bluntly elsewhere too, saying simply, "I want the last cheque I write to bounce."Why Chuck Feeney's quote still genuinely matters todayThe quote remains genuinely relevant in a world where accumulating wealth is frequently presented as the ultimate financial goal. Social media has changed how people think about money too, with luxury homes and expensive holidays constantly visible online, making consumption itself considerably more visible than it once was. Feeney's philosophy offers a genuinely different measure of financial success. Instead of asking how much money someone can accumulate, it asks what that money can actually accomplish. This never meant people should stop saving or building real financial security, which remains genuinely important for housing, education and retirement. The broader point is really about what happens after a person already has enough to live securely.Chuck Feeney became famous for giving away his fortuneFeeney co-founded Duty Free Shoppers with Robert Miller in 1960, starting with one shop in Hawaii. The business grew into a major international retailer, making Feeney genuinely wealthy. Despite that fortune, he maintained a relatively modest lifestyle throughout, famously travelling commercially rather than adopting the extravagant habits often associated with billionaires, and he was known as a genuinely shabby dresser who preferred a simple grilled cheese sandwich over an expensive restaurant meal. Through Atlantic Philanthropies, founded in 1982, Feeney ultimately directed billions of dollars toward universities, hospitals and human rights initiatives, often preferring anonymous donations that avoided drawing attention to himself personally.The "Giving While Living" philosophyFeeney's approach genuinely differed from the traditional model, in which wealthy individuals leave most of their fortune to charity only after death. His philosophy was simple. If money can genuinely help solve a problem today, why actually wait decades to give it away? Atlantic Philanthropies described this approach as Giving While Living, and Feeney genuinely wanted to see the real results of his own philanthropy while he was still around to witness it.What we can genuinely learn from Chuck Feeney's quoteMoney can provide security and real opportunity, but Feeney's life suggests wealth becomes considerably more meaningful once it is treated as a genuine tool rather than an end in itself. Many people quietly increase their own financial target as their income grows, and Feeney's philosophy raises a genuinely useful question, how much is actually enough. There is no universal answer, since the amount needed for real security depends heavily on individual circumstance, but knowing when additional wealth stops genuinely improving your life can help people think considerably more intentionally about money. A person's financial resources can also do more than simply improve their own lifestyle. articles.title: In 2021, Ted Turner gave nearly 80,000 acres of prairie to his ecoagriculture institute; it is now a living laboratory for bison and wetlands
articles.summary: US News: In 2021, Ted Turner handed nearly 80,000 acres of prairie in Nebraska and South Dakota to the Turner Institute of Ecoagriculture, turning McGinley Ran.
articles.body: In 2021, Ted Turner handed nearly 80,000 acres of prairie in Nebraska and South Dakota to the Turner Institute of Ecoagriculture, turning McGinley Ranch into a vast testing ground for conservation and sustainable land management. The 79,292-acre property lies in the Northern Sandhills, where rolling dunes, native grasslands, wetlands and shallow lakes form one of North America’s most distinctive prairie landscapes. Today, about 4,000 American plains bison roam the ranch, helping managers study how native grazing can influence vegetation, soils and biodiversity. More than 60 lakes and ponds, along with streams and wet meadows, provide habitat for a wide range of wildlife while sitting above the Ogallala Aquifer. Rather than simply preserving the land, the Turner Institute uses McGinley as a living laboratory, bringing researchers and land managers together to examine soil health, water systems, wildlife, grazing and sustainable food production on a landscape scale.How is McGinley a living laboratory for bison and wetlandsMcGinley lies within the Sandhills, a landscape shaped by rolling dunes, native grasses, wet meadows and shallow lakes. According to the Turner Institute of Ecoagriculture, the region is the largest grass-stabilised dune system in the Western Hemisphere, giving it an unusual ecological character. More than 60 natural lakes and ponds, along with headwater streams and wet meadow complexes, are spread across the property. Beneath the grasslands is the Ogallala Aquifer, one of the most important groundwater systems in the United States and a key resource for communities and agriculture across the Great Plains. These water features make McGinley important for wildlife while also providing researchers with an opportunity to study how land management influences water systems.The institute’s management approach focuses on maintaining the ecological processes that have long shaped the Sandhills. Its work recognises grazing, fire and climate as important forces in the development of grassland ecosystems. Rather than removing these natural influences, managers are examining how they can be incorporated into modern land management. This allows the property to be used for studying the links between grazing patterns, vegetation, soil health, water infiltration and biodiversity. Wildlife including migratory waterfowl, shorebirds, birds of prey, songbirds, elk, deer, pronghorn, reptiles and small mammals also depend on habitats found across the ranch. McGinley is therefore being managed as an active working landscape where conservation methods can be tested and adjusted over time.Why are 4,000 bison central to McGinley’s conservationAmerican plains bison are at the centre of McGinley’s grassland management. The property manages approximately 4,000 bison, using grazing systems intended to restore the ecological role once played by large native grazers across North America’s prairies. The Turner Institute uses adaptive multi-paddock grazing, rotational grazing and rest periods, alongside the strategic use of fire. Other practices include native grass and pollinator restoration, low-stress animal handling, limited supplemental feeding and reduced dependence on synthetic inputs and fossil fuels. These methods can support healthier soils, improve water infiltration, encourage biodiversity, limit invasive species and strengthen the resilience of native grasslands.Bison management also emphasises animal welfare and natural herd behaviour. The ranch allows calves to remain with their mothers through natural weaning, while management practices are designed to encourage varied grazing patterns and help the animals adapt to the environments in which they evolved. This approach reflects the institute’s broader aim of bringing agricultural production and conservation together rather than treating them as separate objectives. The Turner Institute considers bison an important part of the ecological processes being studied at McGinley, with their grazing helping managers understand how native herbivores can influence plant communities, soils and wider grassland health. Their presence also provides an opportunity to examine how livestock management can contribute to ecological restoration.What makes McGinley a model for environmental sustainabilityMcGinley’s size and relatively intact ecosystems provide researchers with a large-scale setting for studying ecoagriculture. The Turner Institute works with scientists, land managers, universities, industry partners and conservation organisations on questions involving soil health, carbon dynamics, grazing, grassland resilience, water systems, wetlands, native species, pollinators, animal nutrition, animal welfare, climate adaptation and sustainable food production. The aim is not simply to observe ecological changes but to develop practical approaches that could be applied to other working landscapes. Research carried out at McGinley can therefore connect scientific findings with the day-to-day realities of managing large areas of agricultural and natural land.The institute was established with a mission centred on developing, testing and sharing sustainable approaches to ecosystems, agriculture and rural communities. Turner’s wider conservation philosophy has also shaped the project, with an emphasis on finding ways for economic activity and ecological protection to operate together. The institute has worked towards research partnerships with land-grant universities and other agricultural institutions, including South Dakota State University’s Centre of Excellence for Bison Studies. With its combination of thousands of bison, extensive wetlands, native prairie and ongoing research, McGinley functions as both a conservation landscape and a large-scale field laboratory. articles.body: JHANSI: A 27-year-old woman was allegedly strangled to death at a rented house in Jhansi’s Sipri Bazar area, with police suspecting her husband’s involvement.Shivani, also known as Sudha, was found unconscious under a bed at the house near Fauji Tiraha in Awas Vikas Colony on Monday morning. She was taken to Jhansi Medical College, where doctors declared her dead.A postmortem conducted by a panel of doctors confirmed that she had been strangled. articles.body: Alexandr Wang, Meta’s chief AI officer and highest-paid employee recently took a jab at Google’s Gemini after a benchmark data shoed Meta’s latest AU model climbing near the very top of the industry rankings. In a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Wang wrote, “I really hate to say it, but… gemini who? 🚀💨” alongside a performance chart showing Meta’s Muse Spark 1.3 surpassing several Gemini variants on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. According to Artificial Analysis, Muse Spark 1.3 scored 62 points, placing it behind only Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.1 (66) and Claude Opus 5 (63). The model outperformed Google’s Gemini 1.5 Pro and Gemini 1.5 Flash, which scored 61 and 53 respectively.The benchmark behind Alexandr Wang’s dig at GoogleWang's comment was posted in response to a thread from Artificial Analysis announcing that Meta had released Muse Spark 1.3, the company's fourth Muse Spark model release in just five months. According to the benchmark firm, Muse Spark 1.3 (max) — currently in limited preview for Meta's partners — scored 62 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, trailing only Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5 in their top configurations.The publicly available variant, Muse Spark 1.3 (xhigh), scored 61 on the same index, putting it in a tie with GPT-5.6 Sol (max), Grok 4.6 (high), and Claude Opus 5 (high). That score represents a 4-point jump from Muse Spark 1.2's score of 57 in August, and an 8-point gain over Muse Spark 1.1's score of 53 in July. It landed just behind Claude Fable 5.1 (max, 66), Claude Opus 5 (max, 63), and Claude Fable 5 (max, 62).Where the gains came fromAccording to Artificial Analysis, both new Muse Spark variants improved primarily in two areas: agentic task performance and scientific reasoning.On agentic work, Muse Spark 1.3 (xhigh) posted a 12-point gain over Muse Spark 1.2 on the Tau3-Bench Banking evaluation, rising from 35% to 47%, along with a 5-point gain on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (80% to 85%) and a jump in GDPval-AA v2 Elo rating from 1,615 to 1,709. The limited-preview Muse Spark 1.3 (max) variant pushed even further, reaching 52% on Tau3-Bench Banking — the highest score of any model on that specific benchmark — and a GDPval-AA v2 Elo of 1,754. Artificial Analysis noted that Muse Spark 1.3 (max) achieves these higher scores in part by using significantly more reasoning tokens than the xhigh variant, reasoning 62% more on GDPval-AA v2 and 28% more on Tau3-Bench Banking.On scientific reasoning, the standout gain came on CritPt, where the xhigh variant improved 8 points over Muse Spark 1.2, from 18% to 26%. GPQA Diamond rose 4 points, from 90% to 94%, while Humanity's Last Exam and SciCode each posted more modest 2-to-3-point gains.The cost advantageBeyond performance, Muse Spark 1.3 also demonstrated efficiency. The xhigh variant costs about $0.55 per task, significantly lower than GPT‑5.6 Sol and Grok 4.6, which cost nearly double. Analysts noted this places Muse Spark on the “Pareto frontier” for intelligence versus cost, making it one of the most competitive models in terms of value.For those unaware, Meta has released four Muse Spark models in just five months, underscoring its aggressive push in frontier AI.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: In 1996, a young TV reporter bought an abandoned 1830s lighthouse after it failed to sell at auction; he turned its 110-foot tower into an eight-storey home
articles.summary: US News: Standing on Berrow Road in Burnham-on-Sea, Somerset, Burnham High Lighthouse looks more like a giant white chimney than a house. Built for Trinity Hou.
articles.body: Standing on Berrow Road in Burnham-on-Sea, Somerset, Burnham High Lighthouse looks more like a giant white chimney than a house. Built for Trinity House in the 1830s, the circular brick tower was designed by Joseph Nelson to work alongside Burnham’s Low Lighthouse and guide ships through the shifting waters of the Bristol Channel. Sources differ slightly on its height, with figures ranging from about 30 metres to 33 metres, so it is safest to describe the tower as around 110 feet tall. By the 1990s, its working life was coming to an end. The lighthouse was deactivated and sold by Trinity House, eventually passing to a member of the Rothschild family. In 1996, it was put up for auction, where it failed to reach its reserve. Patrick O’Hagan, then a young television journalist who had been sent to cover the sale, became interested enough to investigate the building himself. He eventually bought it and began the much more difficult task of turning a former lighthouse into a home.The lighthouse was little more than an empty shell when Patrick O’Hagan bought itThe tower that O’Hagan acquired was very different from the finished house seen today. The Standard, recounting O’Hagan’s story from his earlier Guardian account, describes the building at the time as an empty shell, with its floors connected by vertical steel ladders. The lighthouse had originally been designed for keepers rather than as a conventional residence, and its compact circular floors meant that almost every aspect of the building had to be reconsidered before it could become a home. The conversion eventually involved architect Elspeth Beard, and the work took years rather than happening immediately after the 1996 purchase. One of the major changes was replacing the ladders with a proper staircase, while the sixth floor was removed during the conversion. The completed property has eight floors, with rooms arranged vertically inside the narrow tower. It includes three bedrooms, a living room and a bathroom fitted with a cast-iron roll-top bath. Rather than trying to hide the building’s former purpose, the renovation retained many of its maritime and historic features, including the original lantern room and Fresnel lenses.Its working life ended in the 1990s, but the tower still acts as a navigational landmarkBurnham High Lighthouse was built in 1832 and originally used a paraffin lamp. Its purpose was closely tied to the difficult coastline around Burnham-on-Sea, where shifting sands and the large tidal range of the Bristol Channel created hazards for ships. The lighthouse was automated in the 20th century, although sources differ on the exact date and on how that automation should be described. The U.S. Lighthouse Society records it as automated in 1920, while local historical material describes it as one of the first lighthouses in England to be automated in the early 1950s. Because of that discrepancy, it is safer simply to say that the lighthouse was automated during the 20th century, rather than calling it Britain’s first automated lighthouse. Its light was eventually deactivated in the 1990s after the Low Lighthouse was recommissioned. The High Lighthouse itself is no longer a functioning lighthouse, but its distinctive red stripe continues to serve as part of a day range used for coastal navigation. The building was also listed Grade II by Historic England on May 31, 1985, recognising its architectural and historic importance.The former lighthouse eventually became a holiday homeO’Hagan’s unusual conversion eventually turned Burnham High Lighthouse into a property that could earn money as well as provide a place to stay. When the lighthouse was marketed for sale in 2018, Country Life reported that it was being operated as a holiday let with an occupancy rate of around 90 per cent and an annual income of about £50,000. Those figures belong specifically to the 2018 property listing and should not be treated as current earnings. At the time, the eight-storey home was being offered with its original lighthouse character intact, including the lantern room and views across the Bristol Channel towards South Wales and Exmoor. The property was listed for £575,000 by Country Life, while other contemporary reporting gave a guide price of £525,000. What makes Burnham High Lighthouse unusual is not simply that an old lighthouse became a house. It is that the building's original form dictated almost everything about the home that came after it. The tower remains narrow, circular and vertically organised, with its former navigation equipment and exterior appearance still recognisable. The structure that once helped ships navigate the Bristol Channel is now a private residence and holiday property, but it has not been stripped of the features that made it a lighthouse in the first place. Nearly two centuries after it was built for Trinity House, Burnham High Lighthouse continues to stand as a landmark on the Somerset coast only now, people climb its stairs to reach a bedroom or a Victorian-style bath rather than to tend a light.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: US reacts to PM Modi-Iran president Pezeshkian meet; issues warning to countries 'helping' Tehran
articles.summary: India News: The US has warned countries against helping Iran evade sanctions, saying those that assist Tehran in generating revenue could themselves face sanction.
articles.body: The US has warned countries against helping Iran evade sanctions, saying those that assist Tehran in generating revenue could themselves face sanctions. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio issued the warning after Prime Minister Narendra Modi met Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) summit in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan.Asked about the PM Modi-Pezeshkian meeting and whether India and Iran were discussing a trade deal, Rubio said, “Well, I don't think there's a trade deal between India and Iran. Obviously there are, you know, countries all develop their own foreign policy, and many countries around the world talk to the Iranian regime.”Rubio acknowledged that several countries maintain contact with Tehran but stressed that Washington would take action against countries that help Iran bypass US sanctions.“No country should be helping Iran evade sanctions. No country should be out there helping them create mechanisms by which they can generate revenue that they will then use to sponsor terrorism and try to build a nuclear weapon,” Rubio said.“And if countries decide to do that, then we're going to have to sanction them, too,” he added.PM Modi's meeting with Pezeshkian came as the Iranian president travelled to Bishkek for the SCO summit, where regional and international issues are expected to dominate discussions.Ahead of his departure, Pezeshkian said Iran did not seek war but would respond “with strength and determination” to any aggression. He also warned that instability in the region would be detrimental to all countries and called for greater cooperation on economic and security issues.“This meeting is very important and most of the leaders of the region will be present in it. In a situation where some international institutions are seeking to create a unified space in the world, this meeting is considered a symbol of the existence of diverse and independent voices in the global arena,” he said.During the meeting with Pezeshkian, Modi is expected to discuss bilateral ties and regional developments. India has consistently called for dialogue and diplomacy to resolve issues in West Asia.PM Modi had also spoken to Pezeshkian in March, when the Iranian president briefed him on developments in the region. articles.title: A West Virginia high school built in 1923 has reopened 103 years later as a 40-room hotel, with its old classrooms turned into guest rooms and gathering spaces
articles.summary: US News: A historic West Virginia high school built in 1923 by Italian stonemasons has reopened its doors 103 years later as a 40-room boutique hotel. Former c.
articles.body: A historic West Virginia high school built in 1923 by Italian stonemasons has reopened its doors 103 years later as a 40-room boutique hotel. Former classrooms have been turned into guest rooms, lounges and shared spaces for visitors. The Hill Hall Hotel, located in downtown Fayetteville, marks the completion of a major restoration of the town’s original stone high school and a nearby midcentury middle school. Developed by real estate firm Mountain Shore Properties, the project has brought new life to a historic school campus that had been closed to the public for more than a decade.According to Travel + Leisure, the hotel is located at the gateway to New River Gorge National Park and Preserve. It combines the building’s historic features with modern, residential-style interiors. The hotel is part of Design Hotels, a portfolio within Marriott Bonvoy. The original high school first opened to students in 1923. It was built by stonemasons who had moved from Piedicavallo, Italy, to Fayette County. The campus served local students for more than 70 years before school consolidation plans led to the main building’s closure in 1999. The middle school later briefly housed a local police station, but the entire complex was closed in 2014.Local developers preserve community heritageThe decision to buy and restore the abandoned school was led by Fayetteville native Stephen Wendell, founder and chief executive officer of Mountain Shore Properties. Wendell’s family has strong connections to the site, with several generations attending the school over the years. A report by industry publication CityBiz said the redevelopment was planned to support the tourism economy created by the nearby national park while protecting an important piece of local history. "Fayetteville has always been more than a gateway to the Gorge, and I hope Hill Hall gives visitors another reason to spend time in town," said Stephen Wendell, founder and chief executive officer of Mountain Shore Properties, in a press statement accompanying the opening. "If someone comes here for the Gorge and ends up staying an extra night, having dinner in town, meeting people who live here, or finding a local business they want to come back to, that's a great outcome for us." The original school’s different room sizes and layouts meant the hotel needed custom designs for each of its 40 guest rooms. Options include standard queen rooms measuring 240 square feet and larger 660-square-foot double king suites with separate living areas and wet bars.Interior styling honours regional culture and family historyMae Pate, head of design at Mountain Shore Properties, led the hotel’s interior design. The project includes features that reflect the school’s history and the culture of the region. Charleston-based architect Aric Margolis served as the architect of record and oversaw the conversion of the historic property with main contractors David E. Looper & Company. According to Mountain Shore Properties, former school hallways and central meeting areas have been turned into lounges, reading corners and social spaces. The main lounge features a large mural by West Virginia artist Nichole Westfall, along with vintage photographs, handmade ceramics and a selection of books. The hotel’s main restaurant, Patsy’s, is named after Wendell’s late grandmother, Pat “Patsy” Wendell. She was an important supporter of historic preservation and helped establish the official Fayetteville Historic District. The restaurant serves Appalachian-inspired dishes and family recipes, including local Clear Water trout and regional meatloaf.The hotel also has a 24-hour guest pantry called Patsy’s Provisions, outdoor fire pits and community gathering spaces. Nearby buildings on the former school campus now include coworking spaces operated through the state-backed Ascend WV initiative. The hotel’s opening comes as visitor numbers to the New River Gorge region continue to grow after the area was officially redesignated as a National Park in late 2020. Guests can easily reach local outfitters offering white-water rafting, rock climbing and mountain biking across the surrounding gorge.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Leonardo DiCaprio helped protect Indonesia’s Leuser Ecosystem, a rare rainforest where elephants, tigers and orangutans still live together
articles.summary: US News: Long before climate campaigns became a fixture of celebrity activism, Leonardo DiCaprio travelled deep into one of the last places on Earth where oran.
articles.body: Long before climate campaigns became a fixture of celebrity activism, Leonardo DiCaprio travelled deep into one of the last places on Earth where orangutans, elephants, tigers and rhinos can still be found within the same connected landscape. His 2016 visit to Indonesia's Leuser Ecosystem lasted only a matter of days, yet it quickly turned a remote stretch of rainforest into an international talking point. He shared an Instagram post, showcasing conservationists and observing endangered wildlife that spread widely online, drawing fresh attention to a forest that scientists and environmental groups had been trying to protect for years. What followed was a debate that reached far beyond wildlife tourism. DiCaprio's warnings about palm oil expansion and habitat loss amplified concerns already being raised by conservation organisations, while Indonesian officials pushed back against parts of his criticism. This highlighted both the global importance of Leuser and the competing pressures shaping its future.Leonardo DiCaprio visited a fragile refuge for Sumatra’s threatened wildlifeThe Leuser Ecosystem covers about 6.5 million acres across the Indonesian island of Sumatra. It is unusual not simply because of its size, but because of the animals that still occupy parts of it.Sumatran orangutans, tigers, rhinos and elephants can all be found within the wider landscape. For conservationists, keeping those species in the same connected habitat matters because each depends on increasingly limited areas of suitable forest.According to Rainforest Action Network (RAN), he said, “The Leonardo DiCaprio Foundation is supporting local partners to establish a mega-fauna sanctuary in the Leuser Ecosystem, the last place on Earth where Sumatran orangutans, tigers, rhinos and elephants coexist in the wild.”DiCaprio's visit brought him into contact with some of that wildlife. Photographs from the trip showed him alongside elephants, while images shared on social media also drew attention to the Sumatran orangutan.The forest itself is under pressure. Agricultural expansion, particularly for palm oil, has altered parts of the landscape, while roads, mining and logging have added other forms of development. Fragmentation can be especially problematic for animals such as elephants, which need room to move between different parts of their range.ID@undefined Caption not available.Palm oil expansion puts Leuser forests under pressurePalm oil was at the heart of DiCaprio's public comments after the trip. The crop is widely used in food and other consumer products, and Indonesia is one of the world's major producers.For conservation organisations working in the Leuser region, the concern was not simply the existence of palm oil production but where plantations were being established and what happened to forests and peatlands as land was cleared.DiCaprio used his social media accounts to argue that expanding plantations were breaking up forest and interfering with elephant movement. He also described the Leuser landscape as a major biodiversity area facing pressure from development.His comments came shortly after he had announced at the World Economic Forum in Davos that the Leonardo DiCaprio Foundation would support organisations working to protect the ecosystem.ID@undefined Caption not available.Why Leuser's forests matter to millions of peopleThe Leuser Ecosystem is important for reasons that extend well beyond its wildlife. Its lowland forests and peatlands hold large quantities of carbon, while the wider watershed provides water and other resources for communities living in the region.Forested catchments also help reduce the impact of floods, landslides and other environmental hazards. Millions of people depend directly on the ecosystem in different ways, making its condition a local issue as well as an international conservation concern.That wider role formed part of the argument made by conservation groups supporting stronger protection. Losing forest in the region would not only reduce habitat for endangered species; it could also affect water supplies, carbon storage and the stability of surrounding landscapes.Government response adds a new twist to the Leuser debateThe reaction from the Indonesian government was more complicated than the supportive response from conservation organisations.As reported by the BBC, Environment and forestry minister Siti Nurbaya said, "My view is that DiCaprio's concerns are both sincere and substantial, and he has certainly acted in good faith," she said.She said the government was addressing problems inherited from previous years, including taking action against companies that breached environmental regulations.The disagreement did not mean the government rejected the importance of the Leuser Ecosystem. Officials said they supported efforts to protect it, even as they objected to some of DiCaprio's public statements.The issue became more pointed when Indonesian immigration authorities suggested that the actor could potentially be prevented from returning to the country if his social media posts were considered provocative or damaging to the government's interests. His tourist visa, officials noted, restricted what he could do while in Indonesia.A short trip became an international conservation storyDiCaprio's two days in the Leuser Ecosystem therefore produced two separate conversations. Conservation organisations saw an opportunity to bring international attention to a landscape containing some of Sumatra's most threatened wildlife. Indonesian authorities, while acknowledging the value of raising awareness, challenged aspects of the picture being presented abroad.The episode also illustrated the difficulty of protecting a large, inhabited landscape where conservation, agriculture and economic development overlap.For the species living there, the issue was much less about the controversy surrounding one visitor. Their survival remained tied to whether enough connected habitat could be retained. In the Leuser Ecosystem, that meant forests, peatlands and wildlife corridors continuing to function as part of one landscape rather than becoming increasingly isolated pieces.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Nepal flash floods: Relatives hold symbolic funerals for thousands missing as toll crosses 1,243
articles.summary: South Asia News: The death toll from devastating flash floods in the Nepal-Tibet region rose to 1,243 on Thursday, as rescue teams battled heavy rain and thick debris .
articles.body: The death toll from devastating flash floods in the Nepal-Tibet region rose to 1,243 on Thursday, as rescue teams battled heavy rain and thick debris while searching for people believed to be trapped in tunnels and underground power facilities along the Bhotekoshi River.Prime Minister Balendra Shah said Nepal must raise the disaster’s connection to climate change with the international community, as families held symbolic funerals for relatives who remain missing following last week’s floods.Speaking at the fifth daily press briefing in Kathmandu, ministry of foreign affairs spokesperson Lok Bahadur Chhetri said authorities had begun conducting temporary burials for victims as search and rescue operations continued around the clock.Chhetri said 11,993 people had been rescued, while 1,114 bodies had been recovered. Around 3,900 people remain unaccounted for, he said, urging relatives of those missing to provide DNA samples at the Nepal Police Hospital in Maharajgunj or their nearest District Police Office to help forensic teams with identification.He also outlined international assistance being provided to Nepal. A 19-member forensic team from India is working with Nepal Police on DNA analysis, while specialised teams and equipment have also arrived from China, Singapore and South Korea to support identification and recovery efforts.Rescue teams from the Nepali Army, Nepal Police and Armed Police Force are working with international specialists from India, China and South Korea to clear mud, debris and boulders from underground hydropower facilities in areas including Langtang, Chilime and Upper Trisuli.According to the ANI report, more than 300 foreign nationals have been safely rescued, while around 590 citizens from 34 countries remain unaccounted for.Working with Chinese authorities, Nepal has also helped evacuate about 2,500 pilgrims returning from Mount Kailash through the Hilsa and Tatopani border crossings and via air routes through Lhasa. Efforts are also underway to clear stranded cargo and assist Nepali nationals near the Kerung border.Addressing Parliament earlier Wednesday, Prime Minister Balendra Shah said the catastrophic August 26 Bhotekoshi River floods, triggered by a high-altitude Himalayan avalanche, underscored the growing threat posed by climate change across the region.Shah said nearly 4,000 people remain missing across Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading, stressing that addressing the effects of climate change requires a collective global effort.As Nepal continues to coordinate international assistance from India, China, the United States, Japan, the Asian Development Bank, the World Bank, the European Union and the United Nations, authorities are deploying available resources toward emergency relief, searches for missing people and long-term recovery.According to Nepal Police, 348 bodies were recovered in Chitwan, 217 in Nawalparasi East, 190 in Nawalparasi West and 155 in Nuwakot. Another 66 bodies were recovered in Gorkha, 59 in Dhading, 45 in Rasuwa and 38 in Tanahu.A total of 7,912 police personnel have been deployed to flood-hit areas to assist with search and rescue operations, distribute relief supplies and manage recovered bodies.Authorities have also published details of 911 unidentified bodies on the Nepal Police website to help families identify missing relatives.Meanwhile, rainwater accumulating inside a hydropower tunnel has created additional difficulties for search and rescue teams working in areas affected by the Bhotekoshi floods, said Dharma Raj Uprety, executive chief of the National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA).Search operations have been particularly challenging because of the hazardous conditions inside the project’s tunnels. Teams from the Nepali Army and Armed Police Force, along with foreign technical experts and project employees, are continuing efforts to locate workers who remain missing.As per the PTI report, Ganesh Karki, former president of the Independent Power Producers’ Association, Nepal (IPPAN), said rescue operations have also been slowed by difficulties transporting heavy equipment to the tunnels.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Former bureaucrat Ashish Joshi was questioned by the Delhi Police Special Cell and was allowed to leave after nine hours, PTI reported on T.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former bureaucrat Ashish Joshi was questioned by the Delhi Police Special Cell and was allowed to leave after nine hours, PTI reported on Thursday.According to sources, Joshi, a former controller of communications in the Department of Telecommunications, had only been called for questioning in connection with an old case on Wednesday. Details of the case were not immediately available.The ex-civil servant was brought to the Special Cell’s office in New Friends Colony around 10 am and released around 7 pm. He was questioned by a team of the Counter Intelligence unit, which recorded his statement."Just got back home. Delhi Special Cell dropped me home. Details later," he posted on X after returning home.The matter came to light after Congress leader Sandeep Dikshit claimed earlier on Wednesday that two Delhi Police personnel had “taken away” Joshi, whom he described as his close friend, from Nehru Park during his morning walk and that his whereabouts were unknown for several hours.According to Dikshit, Joshi, who retired as an additional secretary a few months ago, called him in the morning but he could not answer. When he tried calling back, the phone was switched off.“An eyewitness who was walking with him told the family that two police personnel came and said they had to take Ashish with them for questioning over a recent tweet,” the former MP claimed in a video statement.Dikshit also alleged that lawyers and others sent to the police station were initially unable to get confirmation about Joshi’s whereabouts.A senior police officer, requesting anonymity, maintained that Joshi and his family were duly informed about the case when he was brought in for questioning. articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday spoke to Varanasi District Magistrate Satyendra Kumar and took stock of the flood situation in the.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Thursday spoke to Varanasi District Magistrate Satyendra Kumar and took stock of the flood situation in the city as the rising water level of the Ganga crossed the warning mark amid incessant rainfall.PM Modi, who is also the Member of Parliament from Varanasi, sought detailed information from the district magistrate about the river's water level and the arrangements being made at relief camps for people affected by the floods.The Prime Minister directed the district administration to work on a war footing to provide relief to those affected and ensure that all necessary facilities are made available immediately.He also instructed officials to make immediate arrangements wherever there is an additional requirement for relief material and expedite relief work for affected people.PM Modi further directed the administration to maintain constant vigilance over the flood situation and relief operations and ensure that immediate assistance reaches those affected.The Prime Minister's intervention came as the Ganga continued to rise in Varanasi. According to the Central Water Commission (CWC), the river's water level reached 70.54 metres at the Rajghat gauge site at 6 am on Thursday, crossing the warning level of 70.262 metres. The water level was rising at a rate of 2 cm per hour.The danger level at the site is 71.262 metres, while the highest flood level is 73.901 metres.The district administration has been closely monitoring areas affected by the rising waters of the Ganga and Varuna rivers. On Tuesday, District Magistrate Satyendra Kumar and Varanasi Police Commissioner Mohit Agrawal inspected several flood-affected areas after travelling by an NDRF boat from Namo Ghat.The officials visited Salarpur, Saraiya, Konia, Pul Kohna, Dhelvaria and Sarai Mohana to assess waterlogging and the situation of residents. They also interacted with affected people and assured them of all possible assistance.The district magistrate directed officials to remain on high alert and keep arrangements ready to shift residents to safer locations. He also ordered that boats and other resources remain available for relief and rescue operations.Relief camps at the Primary School in Salarpur and Vidya Vihar Inter College were also inspected. articles.title: Bette Midler started cleaning a neglected New York park in 1995; 30 years later, her group has planted 200,000 trees and built an artificial oyster reef
articles.summary: US News: Bette Midler once spent her mornings clearing parks in Northern Manhattan that the city had all but abandoned. Thirty years later, that early effort h.
articles.body: Bette Midler once spent her mornings clearing parks in Northern Manhattan that the city had all but abandoned. Thirty years later, that early effort has grown into the New York Restoration Project, a charity credited with reshaping green space across all five boroughs. The organisation has planted more than 200,000 trees since 1995, alongside removing over six million pounds of rubbish from parks and gardens citywide. Its work has extended well beyond planting, too. The installation of a 500-foot artificial oyster reef along the Harlem River, built to protect Sherman Creek Park from rising sea levels and storm damage. According to the New York Restoration Project Annual Report 2025, the charity stewards more than 80 acres of parkland and operates over 50 community gardens, with recent projects including a chestnut restoration scheme in Highbridge Park. Three decades after Midler first picked up litter alone, her charity now reaches over 1.6 million New Yorkers.Why did Bette Midler start restoring New York parks in 1995NYRP traces its origins to the mid-1990s, when parks in Northern Manhattan had fallen into serious disrepair. When NYRP began working in Northern Manhattan parks in the mid-1990s, many were informal dumps, overrun with debris. Highbridge Park was among the sites in the worst condition, littered with abandoned rubbish and largely unused by residents.Midler founded the charity that year, with the belief that access to well-maintained green space should not depend on where a person lives. The report notes that the organisation now stewards more than 80 acres of parkland, including Highbridge and Sherman Creek Parks, which it describes as "beloved community spaces with innovative restoration projects."How did NYRP plant 200,000 trees in New York CityTree planting has formed a central part of NYRP's work since its earliest days. The charity has planted more than 200,000 trees, a total the organisation says amounts to more than three times the number of trees in Manhattan. The figure spans both large-scale reforestation projects and smaller community plantings carried out with volunteers across the five boroughs.The pace of that work has continued in recent years. It planted and distributed 4,649 trees during 2025 alone, alongside removing more than 98,000 pounds of rubbish and building or renovating eight new green spaces in underserved neighbourhoods. The charity states that it now owns and operates more than 50 community gardens across New York City.Why did NYRP build a 500-foot oyster reefBeyond tree planting, NYRP has also worked on habitat restoration along the city's waterways. The organisation collaborated with NYC Parks in 2020 to successfully install a living shoreline: a 500-foot artificial oyster reef with expanded marsh grass plantings at Sherman Creek Park on the Harlem River. The project was designed to protect the park from sea level rise and wave action while creating habitat for local wildlife.The report describes the reef as an example of nature-based climate adaptation, noting that the surrounding marsh has developed alongside it. NYRP states that the newly established marsh area is "already matching the existing marsh in its capacity to remove nitrogen pollution," which the charity attributes largely to sewer discharges into the river.How is NYRP restoring American chestnut trees in New YorkNYRP's most recent restoration efforts have extended to species-specific projects as well as broader greening work. According to the Annual Report 2025, the charity has partnered with NYC Parks and the American Chestnut Foundation since 2017 to plant more than 200 blight-resistant hybrid chestnut trees in Highbridge Park, which began producing nuts in 2023. In 2025, this work expanded into the 1,000 Chestnut Challenge and the opening of New York City's first official Chestnut Trail. The organisation says it intends to plant and distribute thousands more trees in 2026, alongside one of its largest community gardens. Reportedly, the charity's work now means over 1.6 million New Yorkers live within a 10-minute walk of an NYRP green space.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: The Tibet-Nepal flood is a warning against defying nature
articles.summary: The catastrophe that began high in the mighty Himalayas on the Tibet-Nepal border is a warning from the world’s youngest, tallest and most volatile mountain range about the dangerous illusion that humans can engineer nature into submission.
articles.body:
Humanity is altering natural ecosystems more rapidly than it is developing an adequate scientific understanding of the consequences. Those alterations are contributing to climate change, which in turn is amplifying the damage to ecosystems. The Nepal-Tibet flood disaster is a stark reminder that humanity must stop trying to bend nature to its will.

The catastrophe that began high in the mighty Himalayas on the Tibet-Nepal border is a warning from the world’s youngest, tallest and most volatile mountain range about the dangerous illusion that humans can engineer nature into submission.

An immense ice-and-rock avalanche sheared off a glacier situated directly along the crest of the international boundary on the Nepalese side, plunged into the China-controlled Tibetan upper basin, and unleashed a devastating torrent that ripped through transboundary rivers, wrecking upstream Chinese infrastructure and leaving a vast trail of death and destruction downstream in Nepal.

The disaster exemplified how human interventions can magnify nature’s fury. Nepal bore no responsibility for the catastrophic flash floods, yet it faced their main brunt. Extensive infrastructure-centered alterations to the upstream river corridor and mountain landscape in the Tibetan border region compounded the downstream effects through physical, structural and operational vulnerabilities.

The tragedy’s central lesson is best summed up by the 1970s American television advertising slogan that became a pop-culture catchphrase: “It’s not nice to fool Mother Nature.”

In the name of development, countries have long sought to redirect river flows, flatten mountains, tame weather and conquer landscapes. Such engineering has undeniably brought energy, water and prosperity. But when it disregards the fundamental logic of natural systems, manageable risks potentially turn into calamitous ones.

The Tibet-Nepal disaster offers the latest illustration of why respecting nature has become an imperative for humanity’s future .

Yet much of the analysis of this disaster in U.S. and international media has focused on climate change while obscuring how human alteration of ecosystems is itself increasing natural hazards and accelerating global warming. Climate change should not become a catch-all explanation that deflects attention from the broader ecological and environmental damage caused by human activity. Climate change is one consequence of these wider human impacts.

The unstable Himalayas are a living geological laboratory. Large-scale construction and river engineering there can significantly compound risk.

Pounded by the slow-motion collision of the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates, the Himalayas remain among the most seismically active and structurally fragile regions on Earth. Their rocks continue to fracture and rise; glaciers expand and retreat; and monsoon rains and freeze-thaw cycles constantly weaken steep valley walls. In such an environment, landslides, cryospheric collapses and flash floods are anything but rare.

The latest catastrophe underscores that inherent instability. But what followed the initial act of nature was shaped as much by human construction as by natural processes.

Natural floodplains, gravel bars and meandering channels act as hydraulic shock absorbers, dissipating energy by allowing water to spread laterally . When they are replaced with concrete embankments, retaining walls, highways, diversion structures and narrowed channels, the river system loses its natural flood buffer. Water is forced into tighter corridors from Tibet, accelerating its speed and increasing its destructive power in Nepal, as a 2022 scientific study had forewarned .

That is exactly how the flood tragedy appears to have unfolded, with extensive embankments, border facilities, highways, intake works and riverbank engineering creating artificial bottlenecks in the upper Tibetan valley. Instead of allowing the floodwaters and debris to disperse naturally, these structures funneled the liquid-rock-mud mass through a narrow gorge, dramatically increasing its velocity before it surged downstream into Nepal’s river basins.

This resulted in devastating consequences. Loose sediment and debris from upstream construction sites were swept into the deluge , creating a dense, hyper-concentrated slurry that smashed bridges, roads, buildings and hydropower infrastructure with enormous kinetic force. Temporary debris dams formed behind bridges and culverts before bursting, releasing secondary flood pulses that were even more destructive than the original surge, as another peer-reviewed study had foreseen.

The tragedy fits into a much broader global pattern. Modern states increasingly pursue projects that seek to reshape natural systems.

China has become the world’s most ambitious practitioner of this approach — from its environmentally damaging Three Gorges Dam and gigantic South-to-North Water Diversion Project to massive weather-modification programs and the colossal super-dam now rising on Tibet’s Yarlung Tsangpo, the world’s highest-altitude major river . Such projects reflect a seductive belief that nature can be bent to the Chinese will.

Complex ecosystems, however, rarely behave like human-made machines. Natural systems function through intricate networks of feedback and balance. Every significant human intervention can alter interconnected natural processes whose cumulative effects may emerge years later or even in places far removed from where the original construction occurred.

The Tibet-Nepal disaster is a strong expression of a universal truth: disrupting one component of a tightly connected natural system creates cascading consequences throughout the whole.

Humanity has entered an age in which its engineering capacity has become extraordinary, but so too has its ability to magnify natural hazards. It is thus imperative for humanity to understand its safe operating space .

Respecting Mother Nature does not mean abandoning development or rejecting engineering. It means recognizing that human ingenuity must work with natural processes rather than against them.

The sustainable path is stewardship, not mastery, of nature. It includes protecting floodplains instead of endlessly constricting rivers, preserving biodiversity instead of simplifying ecosystems, and designing infrastructure that accommodates natural flows rather than reengineering them.

We can keep trying to bend nature to human ambition and greed, or learn to live within nature’s design. The Himalayas have delivered their verdict with clarity.

Brahma Chellaney is the author of nine books, including the award-winning “ Water: Asia’s New Battleground. “
